abstract: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics platforms such as 10x Xenium measure thousands of genes in intact tissue at single-cell resolution, making them attractive for screening which cell populations change between experimental conditions. In small studies, however, apparent changes in cell-type composition can arise from misannotated cells rather than biology, and the reliability of individual cell-type calls is rarely reported. We present SLUICE (Screening Label Uncertainty to Identify Composition Effects), an R/Seurat workflow that classifies each cell by atlas-informed marker scoring and records a per-cell confidence margin and runner-up identity. Each group difference is then tested against three diagnostics: region-specific confidence thresholds, sensitivity analyses that reassign borderline calls, and single-gene driver checks that combine gene co-detection, runner-up identity, and spatial location. Applied to Xenium Prime 5K data from six mice (three traumatic brain injury, three sham) in two contrasting regions, the hippocampus and the optic tract, confidence thresholds differed almost sevenfold between regions (0.17 vs 0.026), showing that a fixed cutoff does not transfer between tissues. Driver checks identified mislabelled populations that margin-based filtering left in place, including Klotho (Kl)-expressing neurons called choroid plexus in the hippocampus and Csf3r-expressing myeloid cells called neutrophils in the optic tract. Excluding the neutrophil panel reduced the number of optic tract categories whose group difference changed direction from five to two (one of which was the Unclassified category), while the major glial populations were stable across all analyses. SLUICE separates robust from fragile composition changes, identifying which shifts merit experimental follow-up before time and tissue are committed to them. Code is available at https://github.com/rebeccasakko/hippocampus-xenium-analysis.
